Explanation: These four cell populations occur in the epidermis and provide structural, pigmentary, antigen-presenting, and sensory functions, respectively.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Epidermal cell types; Cells of the epidermis
Source Section: Skin Structure and Function > Epidermis, PDF p. 4
Notes: Verified: all four are epidermal residents with distinct functions and distinct embryologic origins (keratinocytes/Merkel from surface ectoderm, melanocytes from neural crest, Langerhans from yolk-sac/fetal-liver myeloid progenitors). Retain anatomical-location framing; do not imply shared lineage. Added refs: Martins F et al, J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2026; Van Keymeulen A et al, J Cell Biol 2009.

Explanation: All four connect neighboring cells. Hemidesmosomes instead attach epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cell-to-cell junctions; Intercellular junctions
Source Section: Skin Structure and Function > Epithelial Cell Junctions, PDF pp. 6-11
Notes: Verified: these four are cell-cell junctions; hemidesmosomes are cell-matrix (integrin-based) and correctly excluded. Use standard junction names consistently. Added refs: Green KJ et al, F1000Res 2020; Walko G et al, Cell Tissue Res 2015.

Explanation: A toxin-associated group A streptococcal illness can produce this characteristic rash and accompanying findings. Individual findings are not mandatory or exclusive to scarlet fever.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Scarlet fever; Findings of scarlatina
Source Section: Bacterial Infectious Conditions > Scarlet Fever, PDF p. 38
Notes: Verified. Board-overlap warning: strawberry tongue is shared with Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome; Pastia lines, circumoral pallor and sandpaper rash are specific, so the complete set remains scarlet fever. Do not place the strawberry-tongue tile on a board that also features a Kawasaki/TSS group. Added refs: Dietrich ML, Steele RW, Pediatr Rev 2018; McCrindle BW et al, Circulation 2017 (AHA KD).

Explanation: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxin disrupts desmoglein 1, producing superficial epidermal splitting and fragile skin while typically sparing mucosa.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: SSSS; Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Source Section: Bacterial Infectious Conditions > Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome, PDF p. 43
Notes: Verified. Board-overlap warning: bullous impetigo shares three of four tiles (exfoliative toxin, Dsg1 cleavage, mucosal sparing) because it is the localized end of the same toxin-mediated spectrum; generalized positive Nikolsky distinguishes SSSS. Do not share a board with a bullous impetigo group. Added refs: Stanley JR, Amagai M, N Engl J Med 2006; Amagai M et al, Nat Med 2000.

Explanation: A destructive fascial infection may cause disproportionate pain, gas-related crepitus, bullae, and purple skin discoloration. These are possible warning signs rather than a required four-part presentation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Necrotizing soft tissue infection clues; Necrotizing fasciitis
Source Section: Bacterial Infectious Conditions > Necrotizing Fasciitis, PDF p. 45
Notes: Verified; can-occur wording appropriate. Crepitus (gas present in ~25%) and hemorrhagic bullae (~38%) are late/variable and their absence never excludes the diagnosis; pain out of proportion is the earliest clue. Added refs: Stevens DL, Bryant AE, N Engl J Med 2017; Hua C et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2023.

Explanation: HSV-1 can cause oral lesions, digital infection, keratitis, and encephalitis. This category states capability and does not assign every case exclusively to HSV-1.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: HSV-1 manifestations; Diseases caused by herpes simplex type 1
Source Section: Herpes Simplex and Varicella Infections > HSV-1 and Visual Diagnosis, PDF pp. 49-51
Notes: Verified with can-cause wording. HSV-2 can also cause whitlow, labialis (rare), keratitis (uncommon) and CNS disease (more often meningitis); HSV-1 predominates for keratitis and sporadic encephalitis. Added refs: Ruderfer D, Krilov LR, Pediatr Rev 2015; Steiner I et al, Lancet Neurol 2007.

Explanation: VZV causes primary varicella and can later reactivate as zoster, including ophthalmic and otic forms.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Varicella-zoster virus manifestations; VZV diseases
Source Section: Herpes Simplex and Varicella Infections > Varicella Zoster Virus, PDF pp. 48, 52
Notes: Verified. Intentional parent-subtype overlap (ophthalmicus and oticus/Ramsay Hunt are dermatomal subtypes of zoster) is fair but reduces elegance; board-overlap caution if a dedicated zoster-complications group is used. Added refs: Bubak AN et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026; Kennedy PGE, Gershon AA, Viruses 2018.

Explanation: The source lists these HPV types among those associated with cervical cancer risk. The set is not an exhaustive list of high-risk HPV types.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: High-risk HPV strains; Cervical cancer-associated HPV types
Source Section: Viral Infectious Conditions > Verrucae, PDF p. 55
Notes: Verified: all four are IARC Group 1 (high-risk) types and are included in the nonavalent vaccine; 16 highest risk, 18 second, 31/33 medium-risk. Keep high-risk framing; these are not the usual cause of ordinary cutaneous warts. Added refs: Perkins RB et al, JAMA 2023; Wei F et al, Lancet 2024.

Explanation: These are common, flat, plantar, and anogenital warts associated with different HPV types.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Forms of HPV warts; Verruca subtypes
Source Section: Viral Infectious Conditions > Verruca Subtypes, PDF p. 56
Notes: Verified: vulgaris (HPV 2/27/57), plana (3/10), plantaris (1/2/4), condylomata acuminata (6/11). Shared cause does not imply identical types or transmission routes. Added refs: Rook's Dermatology Handbook, Viral infections 2023; Chin-Hong PV, Reid GE, Clin Transplant 2019 (AST).

Explanation: Candida can infect oral, esophageal, vaginal, and moist intertriginous sites, producing these syndromes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mucocutaneous candidiasis; Candida infections of skin and mucosa
Source Section: Candidal Infections > Mucocutaneous Candidiasis and Candidal Intertrigo, PDF pp. 59-60
Notes: Verified. Most often Candida albicans but not exclusively; do not present albicans as the only species. Added refs: Cornely OA et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2025 (ECMM/ISHAM/ASM); Pappas PG et al, Clin Infect Dis 2016 (IDSA).

Explanation: Dermatophytes can infect body skin, scalp, feet, and hands. These site-specific names describe infections of keratinized tissue.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Site-specific dermatophytoses; Dermatophyte tinea infections
Source Section: Fungal Infectious Conditions > Tinea Corporis, Capitis, and Pedis (includes Manuum), PDF pp. 62-64
Notes: Verified: all four are true dermatophytoses (Trichophyton/Microsporum/Epidermophyton). Do not add tinea versicolor (Malassezia, not a dermatophyte). Added refs: Caplan AS et al, Am Fam Physician 2025; Milam EC et al, JAMA 2016.

Explanation: Malassezia-associated superficial infection causes variably pigmented lesions, has a characteristic yeast-and-hyphae appearance on KOH preparation, and can be treated with selenium sulfide.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pityriasis versicolor; Malassezia skin infection
Source Section: Fungal Infectious Conditions > Tinea Versicolor, PDF p. 66
Notes: Verified; KOH nickname is a standard descriptor (short hyphae plus yeast clusters). Note oral terbinafine/griseofulvin are ineffective against Malassezia. Added refs: Hudson A et al, JAMA 2018; Chen J, Ji C, N Engl J Med 2024; FDA label Selenium Sulfide 2025.

Explanation: The source connects vegetation-related inoculation, spread along lymphatics, cigar-shaped fungal forms, and itraconazole therapy with sporotrichosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis; Rose gardener disease
Source Section: Fungal Infectious Conditions > Sporotrichosis, PDF p. 67
Notes: Verified for the lymphocutaneous form (~70-75% of cases). Rose-thorn exposure is classic not required; cigar-shaped yeast seen in <30% so culture is gold standard. Added refs: Barros MB et al, Clin Microbiol Rev 2011; Qin J, Zhang J, N Engl J Med 2019; Thompson GR et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2021.

Explanation: The source links destructive sinonasal disease with broad fungal hyphae, wide-angle branching, and amphotericin B treatment in mucormycosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis clues; Mucormycosis
Source Section: Fungal Infectious Conditions > Mucormycosis, PDF p. 68
Notes: Verified: pauciseptate (non-/pauci-septate) is accurate per ECMM/MSG and NEJM; broad ribbon-like morphology is more reliable than the historically taught 90-degree wide-angle branching, which can be hard to identify in tissue. Antifungals do not replace urgent surgical debridement. Added refs: Cornely OA et al, Lancet Infect Dis 2019; Kontoyiannis DP, Walsh TJ, N Engl J Med 2026.

Connection Title: Pemphigus vulgaris clinical and biopsy clues
Explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris combines fragile intraepidermal blisters and frequent mucosal disease with keratinocyte separation and a net-like intercellular IgG pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pemphigus vulgaris; Autoimmune desmosomal blistering
Source Section: Autoimmune Blistering Conditions > Pemphigus Vulgaris and Summary, PDF pp. 73, 76
Notes: Verified: suprabasal acantholysis, fishnet/intercellular IgG on DIF, anti-desmoglein 3 +/- 1. Mucosal involvement characteristic but not universal; desmogleins are desmosomal (intra-epidermal), not intradermal. Added refs: Schmidt E et al, Lancet 2019; Kasperkiewicz M et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017.

Connection Title: Bullous pemphigoid clinical and biopsy clues
Explanation: Bullous pemphigoid classically produces firm blisters from separation below the epidermis with linear immunoreactant deposition at the basement membrane zone.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Bullous pemphigoid; Hemidesmosomal autoimmune blistering
Source Section: Autoimmune Blistering Conditions > Bullous Pemphigoid and Summary, PDF pp. 74, 76
Notes: Verified: subepidermal split, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ, anti-BP180/BP230; Nikolsky typically negative (high specificity for pemphigus). Avoid absolute no-mucosa / not-life-threatening wording. Added refs: Schmidt E, Zillikens D, Lancet 2013; Akbarialiabad H et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2025.

Explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is linked to celiac disease and intensely itchy extensor lesions, with granular IgA at dermal papillae; dapsone can control the skin eruption.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Dermatitis herpetiformis; Celiac-associated blistering eruption
Source Section: Autoimmune Blistering Conditions > Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Summary, PDF pp. 75-76
Notes: Verified: cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease; pathognomonic granular IgA in dermal papillae; skin autoantigen is epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) vs intestinal tTG (TG2). Dapsone controls skin but does not replace a gluten-free diet. Added refs: Reunala T et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2021; Antiga E et al, Front Immunol 2019.

Explanation: The source lists these infections among triggers or associations of erythema nodosum, an inflammatory process affecting subcutaneous fat. The association does not mean each infection always causes nodules.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Infectious triggers of erythema nodosum; Infections linked to erythema nodosum
Source Section: Reactive Disease > Erythema Nodosum, PDF p. 78
Notes: Verified: all four are recognized EN triggers (strep is the most common identifiable infectious cause). Competing label granulomatous infection fits coccidioidomycosis/histoplasmosis/TB but NOT streptococcus (pyogenic), so it is not an equally strong complete grouping -- this confirms infectious-trigger as the intended category. Added refs: Perez-Garza DM et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2021; Lionakis MS et al, Nat Rev Immunol 2023.

Explanation: DRESS refers to a delayed drug reaction with an exanthem, eosinophilia, and systemic manifestations. The group describes a characteristic syndrome rather than mandatory findings at every time point.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; DRESS features
Source Section: Reactive Disease > DRESS Syndrome, PDF p. 80
Notes: Verified: latency 2-8 weeks, morbilliform eruption (near-universal), eosinophilia (~52-95%, time-variable), multiorgan involvement (liver most common). Delayed-drug-hypersensitivity is a defensible broader alternate. Added refs: Kroshinsky D et al, N Engl J Med 2024; Wei BM et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2024.

Explanation: The source presents allergic contact dermatitis as a delayed, T-cell-mediated response involving antigen presentation, inflammatory signaling, and intercellular epidermal edema.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Type IV contact hypersensitivity; Allergic contact dermatitis pathway
Source Section: Atopic and Allergic Disease > Allergic Contact Dermatitis, PDF p. 83
Notes: Verified type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity pathway plus its histologic consequence (spongiosis). Spongiosis is a tissue outcome, not an immune effector, which is what narrows this from pure delayed-hypersensitivity to dermatitis. Use epidermal (not dermal) spongiosis wording. Added refs: Kabashima K et al, Nat Rev Immunol 2019; Tong Y et al, Front Immunol 2026.

Explanation: The source associates atopic dermatitis with barrier impairment and type 2 immune features. Elevated IgE and filaggrin dysfunction are associated features rather than universal requirements.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Atopic eczema pathophysiology; Barrier and type 2 inflammation in atopic dermatitis
Source Section: Atopic and Allergic Disease > Atopic Dermatitis, PDF p. 84
Notes: Verified; non-universal wording correct. ~20-30% of patients (intrinsic AD) have normal IgE and no filaggrin defect; IL-4/IL-13 are central (dupilumab target). Added refs: Stander S, N Engl J Med 2021; Langan SM et al, Lancet 2020; Akdis CA, Akdis M, Clin Exp Allergy 2003.

Explanation: Acne arises through interacting follicular obstruction, sebum production, altered shedding, and inflammatory activity involving Cutibacterium acnes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acne mechanisms; Pilosebaceous pathogenesis of acne
Source Section: Pustular Disease > Acne Vulgaris, PDF p. 86
Notes: Verified four interacting factors. Note sources enumerate these slightly differently (some merge plugging with abnormal shedding or list inflammation separately); all four here are individually supported. C. acnes is also a commensal, so presence alone is not diagnostic. Added refs: Williams HC et al, Lancet 2012; Eichenfield DZ et al, JAMA 2021; Moradi Tuchayi S et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015.

Explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa can cause recurrent painful lesions in body folds with tunnels and scarring. The source includes adalimumab as a treatment option.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hidradenitis suppurativa; HS manifestations and therapy
Source Section: Pustular Disease > Hidradenitis Suppurativa, PDF p. 87
Notes: Verified: adalimumab was first biologic approved (PIONEER trials); sinus tracts/scarring reflect established disease; treatment is severity-dependent (secukinumab, bimekizumab now also approved). Added refs: Sabat R et al, Lancet 2025; Kimball AB et al, N Engl J Med 2016.

Explanation: These exposures can provoke flushing or worsen rosacea in susceptible patients. Individual trigger patterns vary.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Rosacea triggers; Rosacea flare triggers
Source Section: Pustular Disease > Rosacea, PDF p. 89
Notes: Verified as recognized triggers; non-specific-flushing-triggers is an acceptable broader alternate. Board-overlap warning: do not place in the same 16-tile board as DERM-025 (also rosacea). Added refs: van Zuuren EJ, N Engl J Med 2017; Powell FC, N Engl J Med 2005.

Explanation: Rosacea can produce vascular facial changes, eye involvement, and phymatous change of the nose. These span phenotypes and need not occur together.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Rosacea manifestations; Clinical phenotypes of rosacea
Source Section: Pustular Disease > Rosacea, PDF p. 89
Notes: Verified across the four NRS subtypes (erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, ocular). Ocular/phymatous are phenotype-specific. Board-overlap warning: do not pair with DERM-024 (rosacea triggers). Added refs: van Zuuren EJ, N Engl J Med 2017; van Zuuren EJ et al, Cochrane 2015.

Explanation: Lichen planus has characteristic surface and microscopic findings and is associated with hepatitis C in some populations. The association is not universal.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Lichen planus; Lichenoid eruption clues
Source Section: Red Plaque Disease > Lichen Planus, PDF p. 91; Histopathology > Hypergranulosis, PDF p. 15
Notes: Verified: Wickham striae, saw-tooth rete ridges, wedge hypergranulosis, band-like interface infiltrate; HCV association (meta-analytic OR ~5.4) varies by population. Not diagnostic requirements. Added refs: Kusari A, Ahluwalia J, N Engl J Med 2018; Boch K et al, Front Med 2021.

Explanation: Pityriasis rosea can begin with a larger initial plaque and then develop scaly lesions in a characteristic truncal pattern, sometimes following a prodrome.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pityriasis rosea; Herald-patch eruption
Source Section: Red Plaque Disease > Pityriasis Rosea, PDF p. 92
Notes: Verified: herald patch (50-90%), collarette scale, Christmas-tree distribution along Langer lines, variable prodrome; associated with HHV-6/7 reactivation (do not overstate a single causative virus). Added refs: Mashoudy KD et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2025; Villalon-Gomez JM, Am Fam Physician 2018.

Explanation: Psoriatic lesions can show retained nuclei in cornified cells, epidermal thickening, neutrophilic microabscesses, and thinning of the granular layer.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Microscopic findings in psoriasis; Psoriatic biopsy features
Source Section: Red Plaque Disease > Psoriasis, PDF p. 93
Notes: Verified characteristic histology (Munro microabscesses near-pathognomonic); findings vary with lesion stage/treatment. Board-overlap warning: do not pair with DERM-029 (also psoriasis). Added refs: Griffiths CEM et al, Lancet 2021; Armstrong AW, Read C, JAMA 2020.

Explanation: Psoriasis is associated with scaly plaques, pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, nail changes, and inflammatory joint disease. These features are not universal.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Clinical psoriasis clues; Psoriasis manifestations
Source Section: Red Plaque Disease > Psoriasis, PDF p. 93
Notes: Verified; psoriatic arthritis affects a subset (~5-20%), nail pitting ~50%. Cross-system (derm/rheum) framing is appropriate. Board-overlap warning: do not pair with DERM-028 (psoriasis histology). Added refs: Armstrong AW et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2025; Armstrong AW, Read C, JAMA 2020.

Connection Title: Risk settings for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Explanation: The source identifies these settings as associated with cutaneous SCC. Chronic wounds and burn scars represent persistent local injury contexts; exposure and immune status provide additional risk pathways.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cutaneous SCC risk factors; Squamous cell skin cancer risk settings
Source Section: Skin Cancer > Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Summary, PDF pp. 96, 99
Notes: Independently verified, including burn scars (Marjolin ulcer: ~92-94% SCC, ~30-year latency). Arsenic is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen; organ-transplant/immunosuppression markedly raises risk. Impaired-wound-healing overlaps the first two tiles but not all four. Added refs: Wysong A, N Engl J Med 2023; Burusapat C et al, J Burn Care Res 2021; NCCN Squamous Cell Skin Cancer 2026.

Explanation: Basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a pearly lesion with visible small vessels and palisading tumor nuclei, with a typically slow local course.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Basal cell carcinoma; BCC clinical and biopsy clues
Source Section: Skin Cancer > Basal Cell Carcinoma, PDF p. 97
Notes: Verified: pearly papule with arborizing telangiectasia (clinical), peripheral palisading (histologic), slow growth with very low metastatic potential. Appearance varies by subtype; slow growth does not preclude local destruction. Added refs: Rubin AI et al, N Engl J Med 2005; Wehner MR, JAMA 2026.

Explanation: The source describes keratoacanthoma as a rapidly enlarging dome-shaped lesion with a keratin-filled center that may regress.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Keratoacanthoma; Rapid crateriform keratinizing lesion
Source Section: Skin Cancer > Keratoacanthoma, PDF p. 98
Notes: Verified: dome-shaped, central keratin plug, rapid growth over 4-6 weeks, possible (not inevitable) regression. Genuine nosologic overlap with well-differentiated/crateriform SCC (often reported as KA-type cSCC); excision/evaluation is standard, so the set must not teach observation over biopsy. Added refs: Tisack A et al, Br J Dermatol 2021; Nagarajan P, J Cutan Pathol 2020.

Explanation: These are four recognized melanoma subtypes distinguished by growth pattern and/or anatomic setting.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Melanoma subtypes; Four major melanoma patterns
Source Section: Melanoma > Variations, PDF p. 102
Notes: Verified four classic subtypes (SSM ~70%, LMM ~15%, NM ~5%, ALM ~1%). Tile correctly uses lentigo maligna MELANOMA (invasive) vs lentigo maligna (in situ). WHO 2018 recognizes additional subtypes (e.g., desmoplastic), but the four-major framing is standard teaching. Acral melanoma occurs in all skin tones. Added refs: Joshi UM et al, JAMA 2025; Long GV et al, Lancet 2023.

Explanation: Glomus tumors arise from the glomus body and classically present as a painful, cold-sensitive, red-blue subungual nodule; the triad of paroxysmal pain, pinpoint tenderness (Love test), and cold hypersensitivity is characteristic.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Glomus tumor; Subungual glomus neoplasm
Source Section: Vascular Tumors > Glomus Tumor, PDF p. 110
Notes: REVISED: original tiles 3 and 4 (Glomus body origin; Thermoregulatory smooth muscle) are two statements of the same concept -- the glomus body is a thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunt made of modified smooth muscle -- so they are not distinct tiles. Replaced Thermoregulatory smooth muscle with Cold hypersensitivity (classic clinical triad feature) to yield four distinct tiles and retain board relevance; explanation updated accordingly. Do not confuse with carotid-body glomus cells (paraganglioma). Added refs: Chen MM et al, JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017; Rook's Dermatology Handbook, Soft-tissue tumours 2023; Lee IJ et al, J Hand Surg Eur Vol 2009.

Explanation: Bacillary angiomatosis is linked to Bartonella and vascular skin lesions, with bacteria demonstrable by a silver stain and a neutrophil-rich inflammatory component.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Bacillary angiomatosis; Bartonella-associated vascular proliferation
Source Section: Vascular Tumors > Bacillary Angiomatosis, PDF p. 112
Notes: Verified (B. henselae/quintana; lobular vascular proliferation with neutrophils around bacterial aggregates; Warthin-Starry positive). Neutrophilic infiltrate is frequent but variable; Warthin-Starry is not specific/always positive. Clinically mimics pyogenic granuloma and Kaposi sarcoma. Added refs: Adal KA et al, N Engl J Med 1994; Cockerell CJ, LeBoit PE, J Am Acad Dermatol 1990.

Explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8, purple lesions, and spindle-cell histology. HIV-associated immune dysfunction is an important risk context rather than a universal feature.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Kaposi sarcoma; HHV-8-associated vascular tumor
Source Section: Vascular Tumors > Kaposi Sarcoma, PDF p. 113
Notes: Verified: HHV-8/KSHV is etiologic in all forms; CD31/CD34/LANA-positive spindle cells; HIV elevates risk up to ~20,000-fold but KS also occurs in classic/endemic/iatrogenic forms. HHV-8 and HIV play distinct roles and are not interchangeable causes. Added refs: Cesarman E et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019; Yarchoan R, Uldrick TS, N Engl J Med 2018; Li JJ et al, Am J Pathol 1996.

Explanation: Acanthosis nigricans produces velvety hyperpigmented plaques, often in folds. It is commonly linked to insulin resistance, while an abrupt presentation can raise concern for a malignant association.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acanthosis nigricans; Benign and malignant acanthosis nigricans associations
Source Section: Benign Dark Skin Lesions > Acanthosis Nigricans, PDF p. 117
Notes: Verified: insulin resistance (benign, common) and malignant AN (abrupt, ~60% gastric adenocarcinoma, TGF-alpha/EGFR driven) are distinct contexts, not features required together. Most cases are benign -- do not imply most signal cancer. Board-overlap warning: shares a paraneoplastic/gastric-cancer axis with DERM-038 (Leser-Trelat); the two frequently co-occur. Added refs: Valejo Coelho MM et al, JAMA Dermatol 2019; Gillespie J et al, Am J Clin Dermatol 2026.

Explanation: The source describes seborrheic keratoses as benign, often pigmented lesions with an adherent appearance that become more common with age. Abrupt eruption of numerous lesions is described as the Leser-Trelat sign.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Seborrheic keratosis; SK appearance and eruptive pattern
Source Section: Benign Dark Skin Lesions > Seborrheic Keratosis, PDF p. 118
Notes: Verified morphology and eruptive Leser-Trelat concept (classically gastric/GI adenocarcinoma). Caveat: the paraneoplastic validity of Leser-Trelat is debated (a large Swedish cohort found no cancer association), so present it as a classic sign, not proven/universal. Board-overlap warning: shares the paraneoplastic/gastric-cancer axis with DERM-037. Added refs: Schwartz RA, J Am Acad Dermatol 1996; Husain Z et al, J Drugs Dermatol 2013; Lindelof B et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 1992.
